Let

\[
P(x)=\prod_{m\ \mathrm{odd}}R_m(x)^{e_m}.
\]

The identity \(R_m(x)R_m(-x)=R_m(x^2-2)\) holds for odd \(m\), since \(x=2\cos\theta\) sends \(x^2-2\) to \(2\cos2\theta\).

For \(D_{15}\), a root \(2\cos(2\pi a/n)\) of \(R_n\) maps to

\[
2\cos\frac{2\pi(15a)}n,
\]

so its primitive denominator becomes \(n/\gcd(n,15)\). Hence

\[
\operatorname{Res}_y(R_n(y),D_{15}(y)-x)
=
\begin{cases}
(x-2)^{\varphi(n)/2},& n\mid 15,\\
R_{n/\gcd(n,15)}(x)^{\varphi(n)/\varphi(n/\gcd(n,15))},& n\nmid 15.
\end{cases}
\]

The factor \(C_{225}=R_{225}\), since \(\deg C_{225}=\varphi(225)/2=60\). The exponent equations forced by the resultant identity give

\[
e_{225}=1,\qquad e_{15}=15,
\]

and no other factor involving primes \(3\) or \(5\). The remaining factors must have indices coprime to \(15\), where the resultant condition is neutral. Their total degree must be

\[
158-60-15\cdot 4=38.
\]

Also \(R_m(2)=(-1)^{\varphi(m)/2}\Phi_m(1)\). Thus \(P(2)=77=7\cdot 11\) forces one \(R_7\) and one \(R_{11}\), contributing degrees \(3+5=8\). The remaining degree \(30\) with value \(1\) is uniquely supplied by \(R_{77}\).

Therefore

\[
\boxed{P(x)=R_7(x)R_{11}(x)R_{15}(x)^{15}R_{77}(x)R_{225}(x)}.
\]

The subscripts are in increasing order.
